name: Representation-technique baselines (HGJ, BCJ, BBSS) and quantum analogues
description: Average-case (random-density-1) subset sum exponents obtained by the representation technique: Howgrave-Graham-Joux 2^{0.337n}, Becker-Coron-Joux 2^{0.291n} (coefficients {-1,0,1}), Bonnetain-Bricout-Schrottenloher-Shen 2^{0.283n} (coefficients {-1,0,1,2}), with quantum 2^{0.218n} (BBSS) and heuristic 2^{0.2400n} classical / 2^{0.1843n} quantum (Li 2025). These are the benchmark exponents any argument via a large number of collisions/representations must meet or exceed. The cited arXiv 2608.07309 is actually Chukhin-Kulikov-Levitskii-Mihajlin, a worst-case quantum k-SUM paper (O~(n^{2k/7}), Subset Sum in 2^{2n/7}); it quotes the classical baselines but is not the source of them.
authors_year_venue: HGJ: Howgrave-Graham and Joux, EUROCRYPT 2010; BCJ: Becker-Coron-Joux, EUROCRYPT 2011; BBSS: Bonnetain-Bricout-Schrottenloher-Shen, ASIACRYPT 2020 (eprint 2020/168, arXiv 2002.05276); Li, Information 16(10):887 (2025); Chukhin-Kulikov-Levitskii-Mihajlin, arXiv 2608.07309 (7 Aug 2026).
status_and_verification: Verified via search snippet: BBSS improves BCJ from O~(2^{0.291n}) to O~(2^{0.283n}) using representations over {-1,0,1,2} and gives quantum O~(2^{0.218n}). Verified in the full text of 2608.07309: quotes 0.283 [BBSS20], 0.218 quantum, Li 0.2400 classical and 0.1843 quantum heuristic, worst-case MITM 2^{n/2}/n^{0.5023} and quantum 2^{n/3} then 2^{2n/7}. HGJ 0.337 is from memory (not in the sources I read): [uncertain] value only recall-based. I did not read the BBSS paper itself, only its abstract/snippets.
key_theorem_or_bound: Classical average-case: HGJ 2^{0.337n} (recall), BCJ 2^{0.291n}, BBSS 2^{0.283n}. Quantum: BJLM 2^{n/3} worst case, BBSS 2^{0.218n} average case, Chukhin et al. worst-case quantum O*(2^{2n/7}) via 7-SUM block reduction (Cor 1.3) and quantum k-SUM O~(n^{Psi_k}), Psi_k = Phi_k - [k=3 mod 7]/9 - [k=6 mod 7]/18, Phi_k = (2k - floor(k/7) - floor((k+3)/7))/6. Pigeonhole Modular ESS in O*(3^{2n/7}) = 2^{0.453n}.
regime_exponents: Average-case exponents 0.337, 0.291, 0.283 (classical), 0.218 (quantum BBSS), vs worst-case baseline 0.5n (MITM) and quantum 0.333n -> 0.2857n. In C1/C2 terms these are what random inputs achieve below 0.311n and 0.5n; the C2 threshold 0.311n is between BCJ 0.291 and HGJ 0.337 (suggestive, no proven link). The AKKN 0.661n threshold concerns bin size, not running-time exponent.
proof_type_and_tools: Probabilistic/heuristic: representation technique (each solution has many representations as sum of two sub-solutions with coefficients in {-1,0,1,2}), modular filtering by a random modulus of size ~ number of representations, multi-level merge tree; analysis relies on the subset-sum random-instance heuristic that partial-sum lists behave like random lists. Quantum versions use quantum walks and Claw finding (Tani) with Johnson graph walks (2608.07309).
quantitative_loss: Constant-in-exponent: exponent reductions arise from the number of representations 2^{Theta(n)} (a 'large collision count' in the representation sense). The loss is that all analyses assume independence of random sums; for adversarial inputs the lists need not be uniformly distributed modulo the chosen modulus, so the exponent bound does not survive worst case (the number of useful representations is not guaranteed).
worst_case_vs_average_case: Average-case (random a_i, density ~1) with heuristic independence. Chukhin et al. state their quantum k-SUM and 2^{2n/7} Subset Sum are worst-case, contrasting with Schrottenloher's single-solution random-instance guarantee. The classical BCJ/BBSS exponents do not transfer to the worst case; the worst-case classical bound remains 2^{n/2}/n^{0.5023}.
coefficient_set: Representation methods use extended sets {-1,0,1} (BCJ) and {-1,0,1,2} (BBSS) to create more representations of the {0,1} solution; worst-case Chukhin et al. quantum k-SUM works with arbitrary integers; the pigeonhole modular variant uses {-1,0,1}.
subset_size_regime: The target solution is Theta(n)-weight (about n/2 ones for density 1); representations split the solution into pairs of Theta(n)-subsets with n/4 ones each, the same size regime as C1's Theta(n)-subsets.
relevance_to_Nc: The representation technique is exactly a controlled count of equal-sum pairs of Theta(n)-subsets: the number of representations of a solution as a sum of two vectors plays the role of a collision count, and BBSS's gain from adding the coefficient 2 corresponds to enlarging the relation space. For random inputs the expected N_c is computable; a proof of C1 would be a worst-case replacement of this expected-count argument. The baselines give the target exponents any N_c-based argument must meet: if N_c >= 2^{cn} collisions can be exploited as representations, the expected time is 2^{0.283n}-like at best for random, 2^{(1/2-eps)n} for worst-case.
relevance_to_Dstar: For random inputs D* (distinct half-sums of a solution's support) is ~2^{n/2} as expected from 2^{n/2} half-subset sums being near-distinct; thus the average-case algorithms operate in the D* large regime, and C2 (hard instances cannot have D* <= 2^{0.311n}) is consistent with them. The 0.311n threshold sits between the BCJ and HGJ exponents, but I found no source tying them. [uncertain] this numerical coincidence may be unrelated.
applicability_gap: Needs: (i) independence/uniformity of subset sums mod a random modulus (fails for structured inputs with high additive energy), (ii) density ~1 randomness, (iii) many representations (needs coefficient sets {-1,0,1,2}, which exploit {0,1}-structure of the solution only for random inputs), and the quantum improvements further need QRAQM. For worst-case {0,1} inputs with polynomial doubling these hypotheses can fail.
counterexample_or_hard_instance_family: Instances where partial-sum lists are far from uniform modulo any modulus: arithmetic progressions/GAP-structured (small doubling, solvable by Randolph-Wegrzycki), and high-energy sets. Random instances at density 1 are the hard distribution for representation algorithms. In 2608.07309 the worst-case quantum bound uses random prime filtering with a union-bound correctness proof (Lemma 3.1) instead of randomness of the input, a worst-case replacement for uniformity.
dependency_chain: HGJ -> BCJ -> BBSS (extended coefficient sets); BBSS -> quantum 0.218 and Li 2025; worst-case branch: Randolph-Wegrzycki worst-case representation (2511.10823) and Chukhin et al. random-prime filtering step. C1/C2 would compose with a mixing dichotomy to replace the heuristic independence step.
constructiveness: Algorithmic: the algorithms are constructive and return a solution; their analysis is heuristic for the classical ones. Chukhin et al.'s algorithm is constructive in the QRAQM model with Claw finding.
lean_formalizable: No for the algorithms; the counting lemma 'number of representations of a vector with weight w as sum of two vectors in {-1,0,1,2}^n of weight w/2' is purely combinatorial and formalizable in a mathlib-free setting.
computational_check: The source papers are asymptotic, with experiments by BBSS on small parameters (largest scale not checked). At n<=40 the repo scripts could count representations of {0,1}-solutions and compare to N_c for random inputs but not test the asymptotic exponents.
next_experiment: Compute, for random density-1 instances at n<=40, the empirical N_c (equal-sum disjoint pairs of n/4-subsets within a solution support) and compare with the BBSS representation count; then compute the same for structured instances to see how far N_c can fall below the random expectation.
open_issues: HGJ 0.337 unverified. The task description says arXiv 2608.07309 contains BBSS/quantum analogues: it does not; it is a separate worst-case quantum k-SUM result and only cites BBSS. Representation analyses remain heuristic; no worst-case proof of any exponent below 0.5n classically except via structure (small doubling, bin dichotomy).
